summary: Adds the PATCH method to HTTP, which lets a client send just the changes to apply to an existing resource. The existing PUT method can only replace a whole document. It is a proposed standard and the origin of the widely used PATCH request.

eli5.summary: Instead of throwing away a whole drawing and handing over a new one, you send a note saying just change the sun to yellow.

questions: how to partially update a resource in http
subtitle: The HTTP method for sending just the changes to a resource, instead of replacing the whole thing.

tldr.problem: PUT can only replace a whole document, and using POST for partial changes works without broad interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5789 defines the PATCH method, whose body is a patch document, identified by a media type, describing the changes to apply to the resource. Servers advertise supported formats in a new Accept-Patch header.
tldr.outcome: PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent, so clients are advised to use conditional requests such as If-Match with an ETag. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5789 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata.

sections.title: Why a New Method
sections.content:
PATCH applies partial modifications to a resource. The RFC says a new method is needed to improve interoperability and prevent errors. PUT is already defined to overwrite a resource with a complete new body, and cannot be reused for partial changes, or proxies, caches, clients and servers may get confused about the result.

POST is already used for this, but without broad interoperability, for one because there is no standard way to discover patch format support. PATCH was mentioned in earlier HTTP specifications but not completely defined.
sections.eli5: PUT means 'swap the whole thing', so it cannot also mean 'fix one small part'. A new word avoids mix-ups.

sections.title: How PATCH Works
sections.content:
PATCH asks that a set of changes in the request entity be applied to the resource named by the Request-URI. The changes are a patch document, identified by a media type. If the resource does not exist, the server MAY create it, depending on the patch document type and permissions.

With PUT, the body is a new version that replaces the stored one. With PATCH, the body is instructions for turning the current version into a new one. PATCH affects the target resource and MAY have side effects on other resources.

The server MUST apply the entire set of changes atomically and never expose a partially modified representation. If the whole patch cannot be applied, it MUST NOT apply any of it. There is no single default patch format that implementations must support, and servers MUST ensure the patch document suits the resource type.
sections.eli5: A PUT hands over a brand new picture. A PATCH hands over a list of fixes, and the server does all of them or none of them.

sections.title: Safety, Idempotence and Collisions
sections.content:
PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent as defined by RFC 2616. A PATCH can be issued in a way that is idempotent, which also helps prevent bad outcomes when two PATCH requests hit the same resource around the same time.

Collisions can be more dangerous than with PUT, because some patch formats must start from a known base point or they corrupt the resource. Clients using such formats SHOULD use a conditional request, for example a strong ETag in an If-Match header. Formats that need no base point, such as appending lines to a log file, need less care.

On caching, cached entries for the Request-URI SHOULD be treated as stale. A PATCH response is cacheable only with explicit freshness information and a Content-Location matching the Request-URI, and then it can answer only GET and HEAD. Entity headers on the request apply only to the patch document, not to the resource.
sections.eli5: If two people fix the same drawing at once, the fixes might clash. So you say 'only fix it if it is still the version I saw'.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
The RFC lists known failures and the status codes that suit them:

  • 400 Bad Request for a malformed patch document.
  • 415 Unsupported Media Type for an unsupported format, which SHOULD include Accept-Patch.
  • 422 Unprocessable Entity when the patch is understood but would, for example, make an XML document not well-formed.
  • 404 Not Found when the patch cannot apply to a non-existent resource.
  • 409 Conflict when the patch does not fit the current state, or when concurrent modifications cannot be queued.
  • 412 Precondition Failed when an If-Match or If-Unmodified-Since precondition fails.

Error bodies SHOULD say enough to explain the problem. After a 409 the client may be able to resend as is, recalculate the patch from the current content, or give up.
sections.eli5: The server answers with a number that says what went wrong: bad note, wrong kind of note, or the drawing changed since you looked.

sections.title: Advertising Support: Accept-Patch
sections.content:
A server can list PATCH in the Allow header of an OPTIONS response. The new response header Accept-Patch lists the patch document media types the server accepts. It SHOULD appear in OPTIONS responses for any resource supporting PATCH, and its presence in a response to any method implies PATCH is allowed on that resource.

The syntax is Accept-Patch = "Accept-Patch" ":" 1#media-type. The RFC's example server answers with Accept-Patch: application/example, text/example. The header was added to the permanent message header registry.
sections.eli5: The server can post a sign listing which kinds of fix-it notes it understands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations are nearly identical to those for PUT: authorizing requests and making sure data is not corrupted in transit or by accidental overwrites. Patched documents may be more likely to be corrupted than fully replaced ones, which conditional requests with ETags and If-Match address. If a response is lost, the client might need a GET, bypassing caches, to see whether the patch was applied.

Virus-scanning intermediaries are complicated because neither the source nor the patch document may be a virus yet the result could be. Servers MUST take precautions so malicious clients cannot consume excessive resources such as CPU or disk I/O through PATCH.
sections.eli5: Be careful that nobody wrecks the drawing by accident, and that nobody keeps the server busy with endless fix requests.
